title: Living in Space: The International Space Station
summary: Astronauts from many countries live and work on the International Space Station, adapting to floating in space while doing science.
poll: Living on a space station would be more exciting than difficult.

versions.title: Living in Space: The International Space Station
versions.text:
Look up at night. You may see a bright dot. It moves fast in the sky. It may be a home in space! It is the International Space Station. Its short name is the ISS.

The ISS goes all the way round Earth. It takes less than two hours. A crew lives and works on it. They are called astronauts.

In space, things do not fall. They float! The crew floats, too. They eat food from packs. They add water to some of it. At night, they sleep in bags. The bags are tied to the wall.

The crew must exercise. They do it for two hours each day. In space, bones and legs do not work hard. So they get weak. Hard work keeps them strong.

Space has no lakes. It has no rain. So the ISS cleans its own water. It is used lots of times. Even sweat is made clean to drink!

The ISS is a lab, too. The crew does tests. The tests are called experiments. They grow plants. They see how the crew can change in space.

Crews come from lots of lands. Some come from Saudi Arabia. They all work as one team.

Look up on a clear night. You may see a bright dot moving fast across the sky. It might be a home in space! It is called the International Space Station, or the ISS.

The ISS is about as big as a football field. It flies around Earth high above the ground. It is about 400 kilometers up. It moves very fast. One trip around the planet takes only about an hour and a half. People live and work on board. They are called astronauts.

In space, things do not fall down. They float! The crew floats too. Their food comes in sealed packs. Some food is dried, so they add water before eating it. At night, they sleep in sleeping bags tied to the wall. That way, they do not drift around.

Each day, the crew must exercise for about two hours. In space, bones and muscles do not have to hold up the body. So they can grow weak. They run on a special machine and lift weights. This keeps them strong.

There is no rain or river in space. So the ISS cleans its water. It uses it again and again. Even sweat is turned into clean drinking water!

The ISS is also a science lab. The crew does experiments. They grow plants and study how the human body changes in space.

Many countries work together on the ISS. Astronauts from Saudi Arabia have worked there. So have astronauts from the United Arab Emirates. As one team, they learn things that help people on Earth.

versions.title: Living in Space: The International Space Station
versions.text:
Look up on a clear night. You may spot a bright dot moving fast across the sky. It might be a home in space! This home is called the International Space Station, or the ISS.

The ISS is about as big as a football field. It circles Earth high above the ground, about 400 kilometers up. It travels very fast. One trip around the planet takes only about an hour and a half. That means the crew sees about 16 sunrises every day! The people on board are called astronauts.

On the station, nothing falls down. Everything floats, including the crew. Their food comes in sealed packs. Some food is dried. Astronauts add water before they eat it. Bread is a problem. Its crumbs could float into machines. So they often eat flat bread instead. At night, they sleep in sleeping bags tied to the wall.

Each day, the crew must exercise for about two hours. In space, bones and muscles do not have to hold up the body. So they slowly grow weaker. Astronauts run on a special treadmill and use a weight machine. This keeps them strong.

There is no rain or river in space. Water is precious. The ISS cleans its water and uses it again and again. It even turns sweat into clean drinking water!

The ISS is also a science lab. Astronauts do experiments. They grow plants. They study how the human body changes in space.

Many countries work together on the ISS. Astronauts from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have worked there too. As one team, they find out things that help people on Earth.

versions.title: Living in Space: The International Space Station
versions.text:
On a clear night, you may spot a bright dot sliding quickly across the sky. It could be the International Space Station, or ISS. The ISS is a home and a science laboratory that circles our planet.

The ISS is about as big as a football field. It was built in space, piece by piece. People have lived on it since the year 2000. It travels in an orbit about 400 kilometers above Earth. It moves so fast that it goes around the planet in about 90 minutes. That means the crew sees about 16 sunrises each day!

On the station, astronauts feel as if they weigh nothing. This is called microgravity. Everything floats, so daily life takes practice. Much of the food is dried and sealed in packs. Astronauts add water before they eat. They often eat flat bread, because crumbs could float into machines. At bedtime, each astronaut zips into a sleeping bag tied to the wall of a tiny room.

In space, bones and muscles do not have to hold up the body. So they grow weaker. To stay healthy, astronauts exercise for about two hours every day. They run on a treadmill, ride a bike, and lift with a weight machine.

Water is heavy to send from Earth. So the station must recycle it. Machines collect sweat and even the water in astronauts' breath. Then they clean it into fresh drinking water.

In the laboratory, astronauts do experiments that cannot be done on Earth. They grow plants and study how the human body changes in space.

The ISS also shows the power of cooperation. Many countries run it together. Astronauts from all over the world have visited. In 2023, astronauts from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates worked on the station.

versions.title: Living in Space: The International Space Station
versions.text:
On a clear night, you may spot a bright dot sliding quickly across the sky. It could be the International Space Station, or ISS, a home and science laboratory that circles our planet.

The ISS is about as big as a football field. It was built in space, piece by piece, starting in 1998, and people have lived on it ever since 2000. It travels in an orbit about 400 kilometers above Earth. It moves so fast that it goes around the planet in about 90 minutes, so the crew sees around 16 sunrises every day!

On the station, astronauts feel weightless. This is called microgravity. Everything floats, so daily life takes practice. Many foods are dried and sealed in packets, and astronauts add water before eating. They often eat flat bread, because crumbs could float into equipment. At bedtime, each astronaut zips into a sleeping bag attached to the wall of a tiny cabin.

Without gravity pulling on them, astronauts' bones and muscles grow weaker. To stay healthy, they exercise for about two hours every day on a treadmill, a bicycle, and a weight machine.

Water is too heavy to send from Earth often, so the station must recycle it. Special machines collect sweat and even the moisture from astronauts' breath, then clean it into fresh drinking water.

As a laboratory, the ISS lets scientists run experiments that are impossible on Earth. Astronauts grow plants, test new materials, and study how the human body changes in space.

The ISS is also an example of cooperation. The United States, Russia, Europe, Japan, and Canada run it together, and astronauts from many countries have visited. In 2023, astronauts from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates worked aboard the station.

versions.title: Living in Space: The International Space Station
versions.text:
On a clear night, you might notice a bright dot sliding quickly across the sky. It could be the International Space Station, or ISS, which is both a home and a science laboratory circling our planet.

The ISS is about as big as a football field. It was assembled in space, piece by piece, starting in 1998, and people have lived aboard it without a break since 2000. The station travels in an orbit about 400 kilometers above Earth at around 28,000 kilometers per hour, circling the planet about every 90 minutes. As a result, the crew sees about 16 sunrises and sunsets each day.

Aboard the station, astronauts experience microgravity, which makes them feel weightless. Because everything floats, everyday tasks take practice. Many foods are dried and sealed in pouches, so astronauts add water before eating. Tortillas often replace bread, since floating crumbs could damage equipment. At bedtime, each astronaut zips into a sleeping bag fastened to the wall of a small cabin, often wearing an eye mask to block the frequent sunrises.

Without gravity pulling on them, astronauts' bones and muscles gradually weaken. To stay healthy, crew members exercise for about two hours daily, using a treadmill with straps that hold them down, an exercise bike, and a special weight machine.

Water is heavy and expensive to launch, so the station must recycle nearly all of it. Machines capture sweat and the moisture from astronauts' breath, then clean it into fresh drinking water.

Inside its laboratory, astronauts conduct experiments that would be impossible on Earth. They grow plants, watch how flames behave without gravity, test new materials, and study how the human body changes during long missions.

Finally, the ISS shows the power of cooperation. The United States, Russia, Europe, Japan, and Canada operate it together, and astronauts from many nations have visited. In 2023, astronauts from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates worked aboard the station.

versions.title: Living in Space: The International Space Station
versions.text:
On a clear night, you might notice a brilliant dot gliding swiftly across the sky. It could be the International Space Station, or ISS, which serves as both a home and a scientific laboratory orbiting our planet.

The ISS is roughly the size of a football field. It was assembled in space, module by module, beginning in 1998, and astronauts have lived aboard it continuously since 2000. The station travels in an orbit about 400 kilometers above Earth at around 28,000 kilometers per hour, circling the planet approximately every 90 minutes. Consequently, the crew witnesses about 16 sunrises and sunsets each day.

Aboard the station, astronauts experience microgravity, which makes them feel weightless because they and the station are constantly falling around Earth together. Because everything floats, ordinary routines require practice. Many foods are dehydrated and sealed in pouches, so astronauts add water before eating. Tortillas often replace bread, since floating crumbs could damage delicate equipment. At bedtime, each astronaut zips into a sleeping bag fastened to the wall of a small private cabin, often wearing an eye mask to block the frequent sunrises.

Without gravity pulling on them, astronauts' bones and muscles gradually weaken. To remain healthy, crew members exercise for about two hours daily, using a treadmill with straps that hold them down, an exercise bicycle, and a specially designed weight machine.

Water is heavy and expensive to launch, so the station must recycle nearly all of it. Machines capture sweat and the moisture from astronauts' breath, then purify it into clean drinking water.

Inside its laboratory, astronauts conduct experiments that would be impossible on Earth. They cultivate plants, observe how flames behave without gravity, test new materials, and study how the human body changes during long missions.

Finally, the ISS demonstrates the power of international cooperation. The United States, Russia, Europe, Japan, and Canada operate it together, and astronauts from many nations have visited. In 2023, astronauts from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates conducted research aboard the station. Nearly four decades earlier, in 1985, a Saudi astronaut had become the first Arab to travel to space.

Aboard the station, astronauts experience microgravity, a condition that makes them feel weightless because they and the station are perpetually falling around Earth together. versions.title: Living in Space: The International Space Station
versions.text:
On a clear night, you might notice a brilliant dot gliding swiftly across the sky, and it could be the International Space Station, or ISS, an extraordinary engineered structure that serves simultaneously as a home and a scientific laboratory orbiting our planet continuously, day and night alike.

The ISS is roughly the size of a football field. It was assembled in space, module by module, beginning in 1998, and astronauts have inhabited it without interruption since 2000. The station travels in an orbit approximately 400 kilometers above Earth at a velocity of around 28,000 kilometers per hour, completing a full circuit of the planet roughly every 90 minutes, which means its rotating crew witnesses approximately 16 sunrises and sunsets during each single day aboard.

Aboard the station, astronauts experience microgravity, a condition that makes them feel entirely weightless because they and the station itself are perpetually falling around Earth together at precisely matched speeds. Since virtually everything floats in this environment, even the most ordinary daily routines require considerable practice before they become manageable. Many foods are dehydrated and sealed in individual pouches, so astronauts must add water before eating them, and tortillas frequently replace ordinary bread, since floating crumbs could infiltrate and damage delicate onboard equipment. At bedtime, each astronaut zips into a sleeping bag fastened securely to the wall of a compact private cabin, often wearing an eye mask to block out the frequent and disorienting sunrises.

Without the constant pull of gravity acting upon them, astronauts' bones and muscles gradually deteriorate over time, losing density and strength. To counteract this effect, crew members exercise for approximately two hours every single day, using a specially modified treadmill fitted with harnesses that hold them firmly in place, a stationary bicycle, and a purpose-built resistance machine that substitutes for conventional weights, which would be useless in weightlessness.

Because water is extraordinarily heavy and correspondingly expensive to launch from Earth, the station must recycle nearly all of it rather than relying on fresh shipments. Sophisticated purification systems capture perspiration, the moisture contained in astronauts' exhaled breath, and other previously used water, then purify all of it into clean, potable drinking water that tastes no different from any other.

Inside its onboard laboratory, astronauts conduct experiments that would be entirely impossible to replicate on Earth's surface. They cultivate plants under controlled conditions, observe how open flames behave in the absence of gravity, evaluate innovative materials for future use, and investigate systematically how the human body changes during extended missions, research that could eventually help future explorers travel safely to the Moon and Mars.

Finally, the ISS demonstrates the remarkable power of sustained international cooperation, since the United States, Russia, Europe, Japan, and Canada operate it collaboratively despite occasional political tensions on Earth, and astronauts representing many different nations have visited over the years. In 2023, astronauts from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates conducted research aboard the station, continuing a legacy that began nearly four decades earlier, in 1985, when a Saudi astronaut became the very first Arab to travel to space.

versions.title: Living in Space: The International Space Station
versions.text:
On a clear night, you might notice a brilliant dot gliding swiftly across the sky, and it could very well be the International Space Station, or ISS, an extraordinary engineered structure that serves simultaneously as a home and a scientific laboratory orbiting our planet continuously, every hour of every day, without pause.

The ISS is roughly the size of a football field. It was assembled in space, module by module, beginning in 1998, and astronauts have inhabited it without interruption since 2000, making it one of humanity's longest continuously occupied engineering projects. The station travels in an orbit approximately 400 kilometers above Earth at a velocity of around 28,000 kilometers per hour, completing a full circuit of the planet roughly every 90 minutes, which means its rotating crew witnesses approximately 16 distinct sunrises and sunsets during each single day aboard the station.

Aboard the station, astronauts experience microgravity, a peculiar condition that makes them feel entirely weightless because they and the station itself are perpetually falling around Earth together at precisely matched speeds, never actually striking the surface below. Since virtually everything floats freely in this environment, even the most ordinary daily routines require considerable practice before they can be performed with any confidence. Many foods are dehydrated and sealed in individual pouches, so astronauts must add water before eating them, and tortillas frequently replace ordinary bread, since floating crumbs could infiltrate and seriously damage delicate onboard equipment. At bedtime, each astronaut zips into a sleeping bag fastened securely to the wall of a compact private cabin, often wearing an eye mask to block out the frequent, disorienting sunrises that would otherwise interrupt their sleep cycle.

Without the constant pull of gravity acting upon them, astronauts' bones and muscles gradually deteriorate over time, steadily losing density and strength in ways that can take months to reverse once the astronaut returns to Earth. To counteract this effect, crew members exercise for approximately two hours every single day, using a specially modified treadmill fitted with harnesses that hold them firmly in place, a stationary bicycle, and a purpose-built resistance machine that substitutes for conventional weights, which would be entirely useless in a weightless environment.

Because water is extraordinarily heavy and correspondingly expensive to launch from Earth's surface, the station must recycle nearly all of it rather than relying on periodic fresh shipments from the ground. Sophisticated purification systems capture perspiration, the moisture contained in astronauts' exhaled breath, and other previously used water, then purify all of it meticulously into clean, potable drinking water that is, by most accounts, indistinguishable from any other.

Inside its onboard laboratory, astronauts conduct experiments that would be entirely impossible to replicate under Earth's surface gravity. They cultivate plants under carefully controlled conditions, observe how open flames behave in the complete absence of gravity, evaluate innovative materials for future industrial and medical use, and systematically investigate how the human body changes during extended missions, research that could eventually help future explorers travel safely to the Moon and, ultimately, to Mars.

Finally, the ISS demonstrates the remarkable power of sustained international cooperation, since the United States, Russia, Europe, Japan, and Canada operate it collaboratively despite occasional political tensions back on Earth, and astronauts representing many different nations have visited the station over the years. In 2023, astronauts from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates conducted research aboard the station, continuing and extending a legacy that began nearly four decades earlier, in 1985, when a Saudi astronaut became the very first Arab in history to travel to space.

keyWords.definition: a building or place where people work for a special purpose
keyWords.example: The weather station on the hill measures the wind every day.

keyWords.definition: a person who is trained to travel and work in space
keyWords.example: The astronaut waved to her family before the rocket launched.

keyWords.definition: to stay up in air or water without sinking or falling
keyWords.example: A beach ball will float on top of the pool.

keyWords.definition: to move your body to make it strong and healthy
keyWords.example: My brother likes to exercise by running in the park after school.

keyWords.definition: a test that scientists do to find out something new
keyWords.example: In our class experiment, we checked which seeds grew fastest.

questions.stem: What is the article mostly about?
options: How people live and work on a station in space
How rockets are built on Earth
Why the Moon is bright at night
How to become a football player
questions.why: The article tells what the ISS is and how astronauts eat, sleep, exercise, use water, and do experiments there.

wrong.B: Rockets are not described in the article.
wrong.C: The article is about the ISS, not the Moon.
wrong.D: A football field is used only to show the size of the ISS.

questions.stem: How long do astronauts exercise each day?
options: About ten minutes
About one week
About two hours
All day and all night

wrong.A: Ten minutes is far less than the article says.
wrong.B: Exercise is done every day, not for a week.
wrong.D: Astronauts also eat, sleep, and do experiments.

options: On soft beds on the floor
In chairs next to the windows
In a small room on Earth
In bags tied to the wall

wrong.A: Things float in space, so a bed on the floor would not work.
wrong.B: The article does not say they sleep in chairs.
wrong.C: Astronauts stay on the station; they do not return to Earth each night.

questions.stem: Read the sentences: "In space, things do not fall. They float!" What does float mean?

To stay up without falling
To break into pieces
To swim in deep water

wrong.C: Nothing in the sentence is about breaking.
wrong.D: Things on the ISS float in the air, not in water.

options: Their bones and muscles can get weak.
The station is too cold for them.
They need to push the station faster.

wrong.D: Astronauts are busy with experiments and other work.

To make the room look nice

The station has a big lake inside.

To describe what astronauts eat

LOW.prompt: Would you like to live on the International Space Station? Explain why or why not using two details from the article.
checklist: I said whether I would like to live on the ISS.
I gave two details from the article.
LOW.modelAnswer: I would like to live on the International Space Station for a little while. On the station, everything can float because astronauts feel like they weigh nothing. Astronauts also do experiments in a laboratory that cannot be done on Earth, which sounds really interesting. I would also have to exercise for two hours every day to keep my bones and muscles strong. I think it would be fun to try, even though it also sounds hard.

Only scientists from one country can work on the ISS.
The ISS is a space home and lab run by many countries.
questions.why: The article covers what the ISS is, how astronauts live there, the science they do, and the cooperation between countries.

wrong.A: Flat bread is used because crumbs float, and it is only a small detail.
wrong.B: The article gives its speed but never says it is the fastest machine.
wrong.C: The article says many countries work on the ISS.

questions.stem: About how long does the ISS take to travel once around Earth?
options: About 16 hours
About 90 minutes
About one day
About 400 minutes
questions.why: The article says the ISS goes around the planet in about 90 minutes.

wrong.A: Sixteen is the number of sunrises each day, not hours.
wrong.C: The ISS circles Earth many times in a day.
wrong.D: Four hundred is the station's height in kilometers, not minutes.

questions.stem: Read the sentences: "On the station, astronauts feel weightless. This is called microgravity." What does microgravity mean?
options: A state of feeling almost weightless
A very small machine used for experiments
A strong force that pulls astronauts to the floor
A kind of food eaten in space
questions.why: The sentence before explains that astronauts feel weightless, and microgravity is the name for that condition.

wrong.B: Microgravity is a condition, not a machine.
wrong.C: In microgravity, astronauts float rather than being pulled to the floor.
wrong.D: Food is described in another part of the paragraph.

questions.stem: Why do astronauts often eat flat bread instead of regular bread?
options: Flat bread is the only bread that can be dried.
Regular bread is too heavy to send to space.
Crumbs from regular bread could float into machines.
Astronauts are not allowed to eat bread at all.
questions.why: The article explains that crumbs could float into machines, so flat bread, which makes fewer crumbs, is used.

wrong.A: The article does not say flat bread is the only bread that can be dried.
wrong.B: Weight is given as a reason for recycling water, not for avoiding bread.

questions.stem: What do the station's machines collect to make clean drinking water?
options: Sweat and the water in their breath
Rain that falls on the solar panels
Ice taken from the Moon
Water from the ocean below
questions.why: The article says machines collect sweat and the water in astronauts' breath and clean it into drinking water.

wrong.B: There is no rain in space.
wrong.C: The article never mentions ice from the Moon.
wrong.D: The station cannot take water from Earth's oceans.

questions.stem: Why is the ISS a useful place for some experiments?
options: It has more scientists than any lab on Earth.
Experiments there are cheaper than on Earth.
Plants grow faster there than anywhere else.
It has microgravity, which is hard to make on Earth.
questions.why: The article says astronauts do experiments that cannot be done on Earth, so the special conditions in space must be the reason.

wrong.A: Only a small crew lives on the ISS.
wrong.B: The article says sending things to space is costly, not cheap.
wrong.C: The article does not say plants grow faster in space.

questions.stem: How does the author organize most of the article?
options: By telling one astronaut's life from childhood
By describing parts of life and work on the station
By listing problems and their solutions in order of date
By comparing the ISS with a city on Earth
questions.why: After introducing the ISS, each paragraph covers one topic: daily life, exercise, water, experiments, and cooperation.

wrong.A: The article does not follow one astronaut's life.
wrong.C: The paragraphs are organized by topic, not by date.
wrong.D: The article does not compare the ISS to a city.

questions.stem: How is eating on the ISS different from eating on Earth?
options: Astronauts eat only one meal each day.
Astronauts eat food grown only on the station.
Much of the food is dried, so water is added.
Astronauts must eat while running on a treadmill.
questions.why: The article explains that much of the food is dried and sealed in packs, and astronauts add water before eating.

wrong.A: The article does not say how many meals astronauts eat.
wrong.B: Astronauts grow plants for experiments, but most food comes in packs.
wrong.D: Exercise and eating are separate activities.

MID.prompt: Choose one challenge of living in microgravity. Explain how astronauts solve it, using evidence from the article.
checklist: I named one challenge of living in microgravity.
I explained how astronauts solve the challenge.
I used evidence from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: One challenge of living in microgravity on the space station is that astronauts' bones and muscles grow weaker because they do not have to hold up the body the way they do on Earth. To solve this problem, astronauts exercise for about two hours every day, running on a treadmill, riding a bike, and lifting with a weight machine to keep their bodies strong. This matters because the station stays in orbit for a long time, so astronauts need to stay healthy during the whole mission. Along with exercising, they also work together with astronauts from many countries in the laboratory, which shows how cooperation helps make life in space possible.

keyWords.definition: having had the water removed, often to make food last longer

The fountain in the square runs continuously, day and night.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?

wrong.A: Exercise is one part of daily life, not the main idea.
wrong.C: The ISS adds to research on Earth; it does not replace Earth's laboratories.

questions.stem: According to the article, why do astronauts feel weightless?

Their special suits remove their weight.
They and the station are always falling around Earth together.
The station spins quickly to cancel gravity.
questions.why: The article explains that astronauts feel weightless because they and the station are constantly falling around Earth together.

wrong.A: The article does not say gravity cannot reach the station; it explains weightlessness by falling.
wrong.B: The article does not mention suits that remove weight.
wrong.D: The article does not say the station spins.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: "Astronauts have lived aboard it continuously since 2000." What does continuously mean?

Only during holidays
Every few years
Sometimes, but not often

wrong.B: The sentence does not mention holidays.
wrong.C: Every few years would mean the station was often empty.

questions.stem: Why does the crew see about 16 sunrises every day?
options: The station has many large windows that face toward the Sun.
The Sun moves faster in space.
Astronauts sleep for only a few minutes at a time.
The station circles Earth about every 90 minutes.

wrong.B: The Sun does not move faster; the station does.
wrong.C: Astronauts sleep in cabins with eye masks; short naps are not the cause.

questions.stem: What can you infer from the fact that people have lived on the ISS continuously since 2000?
options: One crew has stayed on the station for more than twenty years.
New crews arrive to replace crews who return to Earth.
The station has never needed any repairs.
Astronauts no longer need to exercise.
questions.why: No one could stay for so many years, so crews must take turns, with new astronauts arriving before others leave.

wrong.C: The article says nothing about repairs.
wrong.D: The article says astronauts exercise every day.

questions.stem: Why might scientists study flames on the ISS instead of on Earth?
options: Flames act differently without gravity, so they reveal new things.

The station carries more fuel than labs on Earth do.
Flames on the ISS are used to help astronauts cook food.

wrong.D: Food is rehydrated with water, not cooked over flames.

HIGH.prompt: The article calls the ISS an example of international cooperation. Explain why cooperation is necessary for a project like the ISS, using evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained what international cooperation means for the ISS.
I gave at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how the evidence supports my answer.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Cooperation is necessary for a project like the International Space Station because no single nation could continuously maintain such a massive, complex structure on its own. The station was assembled piece by piece from modules built by different countries, and it has been continuously occupied since 2000, which requires many nations to share the cost and responsibility of keeping it running. Astronauts rely on shared systems, such as machines that purify sweat and breath moisture into drinking water, since dehydrated food and heavy water supplies cannot easily be replaced from Earth. The article also notes that astronauts from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates traveled to the station in 2023 to conduct experiments, which shows how countries work together, sharing resources and knowledge, to keep this remarkable laboratory functioning smoothly.
